answer.exemplar: The book was finished years before it was published, and it was held back deliberately until the author had completed the serious novel that would appear with it, which was in fact her last. questions.learningObjective: Explain how the two narrating layers mediate the story.
questions.stem: The herbarium accession register explains that a 1847 novel never narrates directly, so describe the two layers of narration through which its story reaches the reader.

answer.exemplar: The outermost narrator is a visitor who has taken a house in the region and writes an account of what he finds there; much of what we read is his record of a housekeeper's spoken narrative. The second layer is therefore a servant who was present at the events and knows the families well, so the history of two households reaches us through one loyal and not always disinterested witness, and it is framed by an outsider who understands little of it.

questions.explanation: We hear the story from a tenant who records a housekeeper's account, so the history is given twice over and always at second hand. Treating either narrator as the voice of the novel removes the mediation that shapes the book.
questions.hint: One layer writes, the other speaks.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Wuthering Heights and its two layers of narration
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the framing affects what the reader can know.
questions.stem: The invertebrate kick sample sheet carries a note explaining that a 1847 novel never tells us anything outright, so explain how the framing limits and shapes what the reader learns.

answer.exemplar: Because the tale is delivered by a housekeeper to a visitor who records it, the reader receives two accounts of everything: what happened, and how a loyal witness understood it. The witness was present for much of it, yet she has loyalties and judgements of her own, and the visitor understands so little that he repeatedly misreads what he is told. The novel therefore hands over its history already interpreted, and leaves the reader to weigh it.

questions.explanation: The frame makes every fact pass through a loyal witness and an uncomprehending visitor, so the reader must judge the telling as well as the tale. Treating the story as directly given removes the mediation that shapes it.
questions.hint: Everything arrives through two sets of opinions.

questions.stem: Finally, the photography log for the reserve records a question about the impression a set of books made in 1817 but dated 1818, so explain how the misdating shaped the public's sense of what they were reading.

answer.exemplar: Because every dated page in the set read 1818 while the books were bought in the autumn of 1817, readers received them as the newest work on the market, and the erroneous year became part of the impression the books made, placing them at the height of their moment rather than at the end of their author's life. The same displacement explains why the collection has long been treated as a late arrival rather than as the culmination of a long career.

questions.explanation: The misdating presented the books as current and gave them a currency they did not quite have. Reading the effect as a curiosity for bibliographers alone, or as having no bearing on readers, misses how the printed year shaped the reception.
questions.hint: Readers thought they had the newest thing.

answer.exemplar: Because the essay appeared in print only after the author's death, we read it as a document left behind rather than as a statement she had finished and stood behind, and the fragment's breaks then read as the natural limit of a working life cut short rather than as a lapse of care. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Northanger Abbey published late and dated a year later
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the two-year gap between writing and publication meant for the book.
questions.stem: In the species recovery plan draft, a note records that a parody was finished in 1814 and printed in 1817, so explain what that interval meant for the book and for the reputation of the author who wrote it.

answer.exemplar: Three years of shelf time let the author revise the parody in the light of how the fashion it mocks had developed, and let her see the serious novel take shape that would eventually appear beside it. The interval also means the book entered the world after its author's death, so the first readers met a posthumous debut alongside a final novel, and the collection's reputation has had to be reconstructed from the mismatch between those two facts.

questions.explanation: The interval gave time for revision and it also meant the book appeared after its author's death, which has shaped how the pair of volumes have been read since. Reading it as mere delay, or as the cause of the misdating, misses what the gap actually did.
questions.hint: Three years is a long time in a working life.
